articles.title: Tendon cells can rebound from stiffness when returned to softer tissue-like surroundings
articles.description: Researchers at Queen Mary University of London are closer to understanding tendinopathy, a common condition that can cause persistent pain and impaired movement in people and many animals.

articles.title: How online platforms are misaligned with late-career workers
articles.description: The wonders of internet technology and the advent of the gig economy have given hope to many highly skilled workers that their reputations, built up over many years, can help them transition from a traditional office-based job (with all the associated pressures) to freelance work in which they provide clients with similar services but gain more control over their lives.

articles.title: Fungi neutralize spruce defense mechanisms with sugar
articles.description: A research team at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology discovered a previously unknown strategy by which certain fungi neutralize spruce defense compounds. These fungi are introduced into trees by bark beetles, and their success makes it easier for bark beetles to invade the trees.

articles.title: New T. Rex discovery completely counters the long-held image of the dinosaur
articles.description: Tyrannosaurus inhabited western North America during the Cretaceous Period roughly 66 million years ago, near the end of the dinosaur era

articles.title: Snow, monsoons and oceans shift Earth's center of mass each year, satellite tracking shows
articles.description: Seasonal changes redistribute enough water around Earth to shift the planet's center of mass back and forth by fractions of an inch relative to its geometric center. NASA scientists are on the case, tracking the oscillations because Earth's center of mass is a crucial reference point for satellite navigation and elevation measurements.

articles.title: Why you really shouldn't overcook your proteins
articles.description: The development of cooking was a major milestone in the evolution of human civilization because it made food easier to digest and more energy-efficient. Heating food can also kill harmful pathogens and make certain foods taste better. Overcooking, on the other hand, can have adverse effects, particularly on proteins.

articles.title: McKersie legacy honored, examined in inaugural Labor Day lecture
articles.description: The inaugural Robert and Nancy McKersie Labor Day Lecture was given by ILR Dean Alexander Colvin, Ph.D. ’99, on Sept. 4.

articles.description: Forgot your laundry in the washing machine? Sorry, you’re going to have to wash it again.

articles.description: New research charts how preferences have changed over the past 45 years, and where they stand now.

articles.title: Fieldable Quantum Sensors Could Revolutionize Warfighter Safety
articles.description: Johns Hopkins APL scientists are developing a portable quantum sensing platform using nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy that has potential to enable warfighters and others working in contested environments to identify chemical and biological threats before they inflict damage.

articles.title: As ‘2nd Quantum Revolution’ Arrives, University of Texas Researchers Stand Ready
articles.description: From solving specialized problems in quantum computing and developing sensors to training the next generation of quantum researchers, UT experts are meeting the moment. articles.description: The International Communication Association’s decision to elevate human-machine communication to Division status reflects years of leadership from UCF researchers who helped establish the field and create a scholarly home for its growing community.

articles.title: Caffeine pollution could disrupt crustacean defenses against predators
articles.description: While most people are aware of how plastic, arsenic and various industrial chemicals can pollute bodies of water, the effects of caffeine on freshwater environments remain largely unknown. Nonetheless, traces of caffeine, the stimulant contained in coffee and tea, often pass through wastewater treatment systems, entering rivers and streams.

articles.title: 'Lost in Space': Celebrity astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson on his lavish new encyclopedia of the cosmos (interview)

articles.title: Microbes can produce adhesive materials from glucose instead of petroleum
articles.description: KAIST researchers have demonstrated the potential of using microorganisms to produce a bio-based alternative to petroleum-derived materials for hot-melt adhesives (HMAs). These heat-activated glues are widely used in packaging, furniture, electronics and automobiles. Using Escherichia coli, the team produced a new polymer from glucose and demonstrated adhesive performance and thermal properties that support its potential use as an HMA.

articles.title: Three questions: Putting nuclear waste into perspective
articles.description: For decades, one of the major complaints about nuclear power in the United States has been the argument that, after all this time, we still have not come up with a dependable strategy for sequestering high-level radioactive waste, including spent fuel from plant operation. This issue is of such importance that Haruko Wainwright has put it at the center of her research agenda as an Atlantic Richfield Career Development Professor in Energy Studies at MIT and an associate professor in the departments of Nuclear Science and Engineering and Civil and Environmental Engineering.

articles.title: NewHydrogen evaluates Utah site for pilot plant utilizing heat to make hydrogen
articles.description: NewHydrogen is evaluating a Utah energy lab as a potential site for a pilot plant using its heat-driven ThermoLoop hydrogen technology.

articles.title: Radiation monitoring: ORNL builds sensors to detect nuclear material in fuel facilities
articles.description: ORNL has developed a compact radiation detector for continuous, real-time monitoring of nuclear material buildup in facility air ducts.

articles.title: Vox’s Unexplainable explores Scientific American’s biggest unanswered science questions
articles.description: Rachel Feltman joins Vox’s Unexplainable to discuss the enduring mysteries that continue to challenge science

articles.title: Why It Seems Like Great White Sharks Are Overrunning Maine
articles.description: While a bunch of sharks cruising the Maine coast may seem ominous, it’s actually a sign of a conservation success story.

articles.title: The Liftoff Scenario That Terrifies A.I. Doomsayers
articles.description: “Recursive self-improvement” is the idea that artificial intelligence could learn to build and train itself, creating exponential new progress — and risk.

articles.title: Mothers’ Intrusive Thoughts Are Mostly Benign. Lindsay Clancy’s Case Is an Exception.
articles.description: Experts say that after childbirth, intrusive thoughts are common and mostly benign. Lindsay Clancy’s story provides a disturbing exception.

articles.title: First-of-its-kind preventive phage therapy provides promising results against Salmonella
articles.description: The mammalian gut microbiome teems with a delicate balance of bacteria and the viruses that keep them in check, called bacteriophages, or phages. Each bacterial species usually has its own set of phage partners.

articles.title: New simulations link unusual particle diffusion to yielding in soft jammed matter
articles.description: Soft materials such as colloidal suspensions, emulsions, foams and gels often display complex and unusual behaviors compared with ordinary solids or liquids. From a mechanical point of view, for instance, they can resist deformation like solids, but they can also start to flow like liquids when a sufficiently strong external drive is applied. This transition from solid-like to liquid-like behavior, known as "yielding," is central to the physics of soft amorphous materials and to many industrial and biological processes.

articles.title: 'Born-again' star offers rare chance to watch stellar evolution in real time
articles.description: Astronomers have confirmed that one of the fastest-changing stars ever observed has entered a new stage of its evolution, offering a rare opportunity to watch a star's life unfold on human timescales.

articles.title: What China Winning the AI Race Could Look Like
articles.description: Experts say victory in this particular race could come with unrivalled new economic and political powers.

articles.title: Wildfires push endangered Sumatran elephants to brink: Indonesian NGO
articles.description: Critically endangered Sumatran elephants are being pushed closer to the brink as wildfires raze vast swaths of their habitat on the western island of Sumatra, Indonesian conservation group Geopix told AFP on Wednesday.

articles.title: ‘Smart’ Nanoparticles Deliver mRNA Directly to Tumors in New Cancer Therapy
articles.description: The treatment can reprogram immune cells that have been corrupted by the cancer, strengthening the body’s ability to attack.

articles.title: A world 20 light-years away reveals surprisingly organized, Jupiter-like weather
articles.description: Scientists from Trinity College Dublin have developed a way to unravel changing weather patterns on distant worlds. Using this approach, they discovered that the weather on a well-studied brown dwarf, SIMP 0136, previously linked to northern lights-like phenomena, is largely shaped by just two dominant processes: changes in temperature and the vertical structure of its clouds.

articles.title: Study finds violence affects millions across US with links to health, economic hardship
articles.description: A new national study reveals the widespread reach of violence across the United States, finding that more than half of U.S. adults have experienced physical violence and nearly half have experienced sexual violence in their lifetimes. The U.S. National Study on Violence Experiences Across the Lifespan (USVEX) also shows stark disparities in who experiences violence and how closely violence is linked to economic hardship, mental health and substance use.

articles.title: UK mathematician debunks myth around Parthenon’s optical illusions
articles.description: Study challenges belief that temple’s curves were designed to correct optical illusions that would have ruined its clean lines A mathematician has uncovered what may be one of the longest-running myths in history after studying optical illusions and the Parthenon, the famed Greek temple that overlooks Athens. Scholars have marvelled at the building on the Acropolis hill for more than 2,000 years and heaped praise on its architects for their clever use of geometry. Its subtle curves are said to correct optical illusions that would have otherwise ruined the Parthenon’s clean lines. Continue reading...

articles.title: Chimpanzees give youngsters the tools to learn tricky techniques
articles.description: Two-thirds of a century after Jane Goodall observed "David Greybeard" break off a twig to fashion a fishing rod for termites, researchers following in her footsteps have found that adult chimpanzees in Senegal literally hand youngsters the tools for learning.

articles.title: Letters Without Limits: Rose Tuck
articles.description: Letters Without Limits, founded by students at Johns Hopkins and Brown University, connects volunteers with palliative care and hospice patients to co-create "Legacy Letters." These letters capture memories, values and lessons that patients wish to share, preserving stories that might otherwise be lost. By honoring these voices and preserving legacies, Letters Without Limits hopes to affirm the central role of humanism in medicine, reminding us that every patient is more than their illness and that their voices deserve to be heard. As you read these powerful Legacy Letters, we invite you to pause, reflect and recognize the beauty in every life. Interviewer's note Rose Tuck is an optimistic individual. I admire her love for taking care of others and spending time with her family. It was a pleasure to learn about her life and listen to the many stories she has to share. Her authentic life-view is especially inspiring to me. Early life I was born in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania on December 8, 1942. My mother was a domestic worker, and my father was a steelworker. I had five siblings, and we had a pleasant childhood. We managed to stay together, go to school, accept responsibilities and accept jobs that we wanted. Growing up, I always did what I was told to do. I always wanted to be a leader. I never wanted to be a follower. Even when I was younger, I never wanted to be a follower. When I was going to high school, in the 12th grade, these guys came up to us and asked if we wanted to smoke. I said all right. I started coughing. Threw it down. Stepped on it. That's it, no more. At graduation they were having parties. Everyone was trying vodka, and I stuck my tongue in some one time. Never, no more. When we were all going out together, I was the driver. I never let someone get behind the wheel if they were drinking. Everybody's different. Career I was looking in the News-American paper, and there were jobs for the state of Maryland. I went to apply for the job. I was 24. They said that they wanted the first people they hired to be 26. I haven't done anything wrong. I'm gonna do something wrong. I asked my sister if she knew anything about make-up. She said tomorrow we're going to Murphy. I went, and I got all that stuff. So I made my face back up, I went right back to the same job, and I talked to the same woman. She said I have to be 26, and I said I was 26. So I got the job, and I stayed on the job. When I went to personnel for retirement, the lady said that I was born in '40. I said someone made a mistake. I was born in '42. She changed it. I worked for the state of Maryland, with the intellectually disabled, for 40 years. We enjoyed something that we wanted to do, and we were blessed by doing it. We made a lot of friends, met a lot of people that we cared about and we took care of them proper. My family I was married for 34 years. When we started dating, I said that we're gonna wait a while. We're gonna wait three years. So after three years, everything went well, and I said yes. We were both 36, and we got married. He passed away in 2009. I got a sister who is 95, and we get along fine. We have a knit family. We have a family reunion every September 6, and our entire family comes together.We meet together every Thanksgiving, Christmas and September 6. We all enjoy each other. Most of my family, the younger generation, they're involved in church. I got a very pleasant, very nice daughter. My daughter is young, and she has a lot of years ahead of her. I hope if anything happens to me, she remains who she is. I hope she remains comfortable in herself. Her do's and don't's are her concern. She comes every other day. She takes my clothes home, does them and takes them back. My brother in law comes with her. He's such a lovely person. He does the laundry and cleaning and goes to the store with my daughter. In our home, I don't have to do anything but take care of myself. I'm grateful for that. We get along fine, the three of us. That's the way life is with me. Helping others I take care of everybody. I go take people to the store. I take a lot of people to bingo. If people call me and ask me to go to hospital appointments, I go with them. That's what I did every day before I got sick, and I intend to continue as I get better. It's something that God gave me. It's a gift that he gave me, and I accepted it. It's something that's just in me. It's been like that for me ever since I was 19 years old. Final message I tell everyone to live your life the best you can and to the best of your knowledge. Follow your steps. Don't start something and then stop. If it's something you like, you do it. If it's not, pursue what you want to do with your life. Follow your dreams. Do what you think is right. Nobody tells you what to do. With love, Rose Tuck

articles.title: SGA discusses DOE's "National Call to Action," introduces philanthropy legislation
articles.description: On Tuesday, September 15 the Hopkins Student Government Association (SGA) convened for their fourth weekly general body meeting (GBM) of the academic year. The meeting began with a presentation from the SGA Judiciary Committee outlining their responsibilities. The five-member court, which currently contains two vacancies, reviews formal complaints, interprets SGA governing documents, issues binding decisions and serves as the final avenue of appeal for SGA matters. It also hears appeals of election rulings issued by the Committee on Student Elections. Civic Engagement Committee Chair Jackson Morris presented a comprehensive view of the U.S. Department of Education's recent "National Call to Action" with the hope that the SGA can make an informed decision about whether the issue is important enough to act on. The letter, sent by U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon to U.S. university presidents on August 3, asks universities to publish a statement by the end of 2026 addressing seven topics: transparency and merit in admissions, free speech and open inquiry, intellectual pluralism and academic vitality, affordability and student outcomes, academic rigor in the age of artificial intelligence, protection of research from foreign influences and the prioritization of U.S. interests. Morris acknowledged that many of the letters' stated goals, such as protecting open debate and tuition transparency, were worthwhile. However, he was concerned about the final two questions regarding foreign influence and U.S. exceptionalism as well as their potential implications for international and immigrant members of the Hopkins community. "While the words 'international' and 'immigrant' do not appear in this letter, it is impossible to ignore [them] in the context of this administration's attacks on U.S. citizens and limits on noncitizen and international student enrollment, work authorization and subsequent residency and citizenship," Morris said. Morris argued that the University's response will be better and much more representative of the community if students play a role in crafting it. After discussion, members proposed meeting with the Office of the President and the Office of the Provost, conducting an undergraduate survey and contacting registered student organization (RSO) leaders to gather opinions. SGA did not reach a formal decision on the issue during this meeting. Morris offered to serve as the point of contact for members interested in developing a more concrete action plan to be voted on. Following this discussion, SGA passed a bill for a prospective student organization fair on October 2 on the Beach. The event will give proposed organizations an opportunity to recruit members needed to apply for recognition. Organizers plan to invite more than 200 students who attended information sessions about creating new organizations, and provide ice cream at the fair. Senators also passed the Accountability Act, which changes attendance and accountability procedures for SGA members. Senator Mamadou Thiam introduced a bill requesting partial funding for Phi Delta Theta's fourth annual Crab Fest during Family Weekend. Fraternity Representative Reagan Sam claimed the event served over 500 people last year and usually raises about $10,000 for the LiveLikeLou Foundation, which supports amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) research. Some senators' were skeptical of the event, noting that 12 bushels of crabs remained after last year's event. Lastly, public member Sean Durkis-Dervogne proposed the Budget Reporting Act. The bill would require the treasurer to publish a more detailed summary of SGA's spending each semester. The reports would break spending down by RSO and expense categories without identifying the allocation received by every individual organization.

articles.title: Our picks of art released in summer 2026
articles.description: The Arts & Entertainment section presents our picks of art released during the summer. We hope you check them out! Estelle Chen: Sophie Calle's The Sleepers installation at the Museum of Modern Art Many artists are inspired by dreams. Sophie Calle's The Sleepers is inspired by sleep. The state of sleep is precisely that thing most vulnerable and unaware, which is exactly what prompted French conceptual artist Sophie Calle to invite 27 people into her bed over the course of eight days in 1979. She documented their bed habits; she fed them, questioned them and photographed them while they were sleeping. This amalgamation of art, social experiment and semi-breach of privacy is an ongoing installation which opened last spring at the Museum of Modern Art. The Sleepers occupies the walls of an entire exhibition room. The people in her bed include strangers, friends and Calle's own mother. During each one's 8-hour shift, she takes a photo every hour. She notes what they wear to bed and how they arrange the sheets. No detail is too minute. Traversing the installation this summer, I felt that I was both trespassing into something intensely private and witnessing the results of an ordered scientific procedure. Both feelings speak of a special care - Calle didn't consider herself an artist at the time, but rather someone with a peculiar interest, attentively making public some of our most private experiences. Yet Calle kept her distance from the sleepers, with "an attraction, not to know somebody's life, but to know details." The result is a strange beauty. The photos capture the comfort of rest through the frankness of strangers, at once intimate and the alien. Saffron Hallett: the Musical Bodies exhibit at The Metropolitan Museum of Art: Available from June 7 to Sept. 27, this exhibit covers the complex connections between music and the human form through a unique display of instruments, art and interactive experiences. Upon entering, the viewer sees anthropomorphic instruments from early civilizations, highlighting the use of instruments and music to capture age-old customs and their place as historical artifacts. Looped videos of dance and singing performances depict the function of the body as the first musical instrument and its many modes of expression. A display of instruments, like a 360-degree keyboard and a theremin, are accompanied with headphones to listen to performances and directly experience the sounds. For even greater immersivity, visitors can choose to use the giant floor keyboard similar to that used in the movie Big . The following section introduces pieces that reflect personal identities - like Prince's Symbol Guitar - and cultural practices, such as the vast array of European pochettes (thin, portable fiddles used by dance masters who served aristocracy). The final exhibits focus on the role of music in two important factors of life: love and death. From a painted harpsichord to porcelain figurines, these pieces exemplify Darwin's own ideas on music in sexual selection such as bird song. Meanwhile, the juxtaposition with death in the accompanying room further stresses the presence of music throughout and beyond life. The most eye-catching piece in this room is the full Día de los Muertos drum kit of Alex González of Mexican band Maná - with all its skulls and vibrant turquoise color scheme. This free exhibit raises the bar in musical representation in museums by unveiling the rich tapestry between facets of human life and this magical art form, utilizing 130 pieces spanning 4,000 years of history in ways that immerse visitors of all ages. Finnigan Keane: We Burned So Bright by TJ Klune While the cover of the book is beautiful, it wasn't what caught my attention. I had read TJ Klune in the past, reading both books in the Cerulean Chronicles series - House in the Cerulean Sea and Somewhere Beyond the Sea - and I thoroughly enjoyed both books. But, one thing to know about TJ Klune is his books are usually over 400 pages long! So, when I saw that his newest release We Burned So Bright , was merely 176 pages long, I was incredibly surprised. Although the length of the book has been a subject of much controversy and debate on the Internet, I think it makes the book all the more powerful. I won't spoil the book, as I think it is an incredible book that everyone should read it. But, I will attach a snippet of the summary from the back of the book , as Klune words it more beautifully than I ever could: "Husbands Don and Rodney have lived a good long life. Together they've experienced the highest highs of love and family, and lows so low that they felt like the end of the world. Now, the world is ending for real. A wandering black hole is coming for Earth and in a month everything and everyone they've ever known will be gone. Suddenly, after 40 years together, Don and Rodney are out of time. They're in a race against the clock to make it from Maine to Washington State to take care of some unfinished business before it's all over." As one can see, the incredibly short length of the book makes sense, making it feel like both the characters and the author himself are running out of time. Despite it appearing as such a sad book (and trust me, it is), there are a lot of beautiful, bizarre and absurd moments that get slapped in there. From impromptu weddings to the small, intimate moments Don and Rodney have, We Burned So Bright shows that not every moment before the end has to be depressing. River Phan: Rose of Nevada directed by Mark Jenkin In Rose of Nevada , two fishermen crew a mysterious boat and find themselves transported back 30 years ago as the now-deceased men who previously manned the vessel. Nick (George McKay) longs to return to his family once he realizes they've been displaced in time. Meanwhile, Liam (Callum Turner) enjoys his new role; back in their reality, he's a wayward worker with no ties to anyone or anything, but in the '90s, he's a father like present-day Nick. While Nick tries to sail the boat back to his time, Liam settles into the town and his new life. Their personal motives complicate the two fishermen's values and sense of duty as it becomes clear the small port town depends on them for economic survival. Nick, now constantly plagued by nightmares and visions of the original crew, confronts Liam about their disturbing situation as he descends deeper into despair while Liam solidly upholds his new identity. Their confrontation turns physical; the two men seem to be at irreconcilable odds. Shot entirely in 16mm, Rose of Nevada fills the screen with an overwhelming sense of smothering, textured nostalgia: a ghost story haunted by an abandoned past revived against the wishes of its new inhabitants. As a sad, slow picture, Rose of Nevada methodically conveys the means necessary to letting go as the only choice before memory inevitably flees. Selven Ren: The Odyssey directed Christopher Nolan A story nearly three millennia old. An Oscar-winning filmmaker. And, for the first, time, a feature shot entirely with IMAX film cameras . Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey (2026) turns Homer's ancient Greek epic into a massive 172-minute adventure. The film follows Odysseus (Matt Damon) as he struggles home to Ithaca after the Trojan War. Across the sea, his wife Penelope (Anne Hathaway) is surrounded by suitors competing for her hand and his throne. Meanwhile, their son Telemachus (Tom Holland) sets out in search of his father who never returned. With angry gods, terrifying monsters, brutal wars and a perilous journey at its core, Homer's story already has everything a fantasy fan could ask for. But, Nolan's ambition goes far beyond simply bringing a well-known ancient hero to the big screen. The film offers a unique, Nolan-esque take on Odysseus, shedding light on the darker side of the heroism that has defined The Odyssey for thousands of years. Nolan's Odysseus is less a legend than a survivor - a man driven by instincts, cunning and everything he has suffered along the way. And then, there is the music. Reuniting with Nolan after Tenet and Oppenheimer , renowned composer Ludwig Göransson delivers one of the film's most striking creative strengths. He blends music with his unique sound design to create a distinctive sonic landscape that gives us a vivid sense of the character's inner world. Whether you're a Nolan fan, a mythology buff or simply looking for a place to spend a few hours, The Odyssey gives you plenty of reasons to make the trip to IMAX. Steve Wang: Lost Weekend by Phoebe Bridgers In the six years since her last solo album , Phoebe Bridgers' career seems to have taken an impossibly sharp turn toward the mainstream: she was touring the world after Punisher took off, and then again with her supergroup boygenius after the release of The Record , and then again opening for Taylor Swift ... all while processing the passing of her father in early 2023. It is not surprising then that her new album, Lost Weekend , is one of movement and experimentation for Bridgers. She does not simply settle with the ambient, droning indie-folk that made her popular, instead opting to incorporate new influences all the way from bluegrass to indietronica. The album opens with Bridgers at her father's funeral " crying in a suit and tie " while she explores her relationship with dissociation in front of an appropriately sparse, piano-led instrumental. After nearly a minute of outro, the album's lead single " Lost Boys " opens to a more uptempo tone and horn lines from Bright Eyes' Nate Walcott reminiscent of " Kyoto ." As the album continues to unfurl, we see some of Bridgers' signature deathly potent one-liners on " The Governor's Waltz " with " you're next to me / I'm next to nothing " and " being myself wasn't easy / do it for me " standing out, a surprisingly joyous love song to Bo Burnham in " Bobby " and a massively epic buildup at the end of " I Can't Wait ." In all, Bridgers manages to come back from her hiatus with a beautifully intimate album that is both wonderfully celebratory yet haunted with grief and sorrow.

articles.title: Bookstore reopening success: a shared space
articles.description: On Thursday September 10th, Hopkins held the Campus Store Grand Reopening Celebration , an event that welcomed individuals to see the new layout and amenities of the campus bookstore. Major store renovations took place during the summer months of 2026 after Follett Higher Education Group assumed operations from Barnes and Noble in 2025. On Thursday, over 100 students lined up outside the store waiting for the 11 A.M. start. When the doors were opened, attendees were treated to sugar cookies with Hopkins logos, a photobooth, and a popcorn machine. Alexis Daniels , a Washington D.C. based event planner, brought the popcorn machine in addition to the balloon garlands she made for the event. In an interview with The News-Letter, Daniels described her experience working with Hopkins. "This space is really nice," she said. "It was really good working with Hopkins." Daniels has worked with other universities, including George Washington University, to plan events in the past. Kristin Forbes, who joined Hopkins with Follett Education, is the new store manager. She has been working on the space's renovation for over a year. In an interview with The News-Letter, she described her enthusiastism about how the changes to space will affect the atmosphere. "We really wanted to make this feel like a store for the students," Forbes said. "You guys are always welcome here." Forbes explained that although the person-oriented design of the store prioritized student experience, the store's renovations were meant to extend beyond student needs. "You know how Hopkins has security all around the building," she said. "They come here with regularity. Everybody's welcome: community, staff, faculty, students." Officer Iona Brown was working as security outside the store during the celebration. In an interview with The News-Letter, she confirmed Forbes' description of the store as a welcoming space for security staff to recharge. "It's a nice, chill, cool spot for us to go sit down as security guards," she said. "We can charge our phones, relax and get some air." Students, seasoned and new at Hopkins, had an overwhelmingly positive view of the reconnations. Some of these renovations included the adding of a Changing room, the revamping of a technology sales and J-card and IT service and increased seating on the second floor. Savannah Anderson, a senior at Hopkins, was the last person to receive a complimentary gift bag as the 100th person in line. In an interview with The News-Letter, she described her excitement about the bookstore. "I think the new bookstore is great," she said. "I'm glad I get to experience this during my senior year before I graduate." Anthony Lu, a freshman at Hopkins, visited the bookstore in December before he began classes at Hopkins. In an interview with The News-Letter, he explained that the store looked significantly improved and admired the modern look. "When I first came here, the bookstore did look old," he said. "I like the layout now. Something I especially like is the Hello Kitty merchandise." Attendees of the event were given discounts to apply to their purchases and shopped the bookstore aisles shortly after the celebration began. Many perused the merchandise, which has been newly organized. Additionally, under Follet Education, Hopkins affiliates will be able to customize their own merchandise online. Whitney Taylor, a professional staff member of 14 years at Hopkins, was similarly impressed by the store's renovation. In an interview with The News-Letter, she described her curiosity about how the bookstore might be affected by Follet Education's takeover and her eventual satisfaction. "I love the look: nice, new and fresh," she said. "I really hope it does well." In addition to housing merchandise and providing study space, the bookstore is expected to host events like book signings, live music and art exhibitions.

articles.title: Transparency and trust are the foundations of every successful research partnership, report suggests
articles.description: According to research by the IfM Bonn, strengthening research collaboration between universities and businesses requires regional technology transfer networks in which technology transfer offices at universities and research institutions, as well as chambers of commerce and industry, trade associations, chambers of crafts, business-related networks and financial intermediaries, all play an active role. In this way, networking opportunities could be pooled and examples of good practice highlighted.

articles.title: How high turnover rates in Tanzania's agro-dealer sector affect farmer fertilizer adoption
articles.description: Smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa adopt agricultural inputs, including fertilizer, at low rates, contributing to low agricultural productivity. Previous research has shown that insufficient information and distrust in the quality of products for sale in local markets are among the reasons for low rates of fertilizer adoption and application. In a new study published in the American Journal of Agricultural Economics, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers examined the agricultural marketplace in Tanzania, finding that frequent turnover among local agro-dealers affects farmer perceptions of product quality and has implications for broader market functioning.

articles.title: A new mechanism for reading extra-long genes in neurons
articles.description: Neurons in humans and other mammals express many exceptionally long genes, ranging from more than 100 kbp to more than 2 Mbp, that are important for forming synapses and neural circuits. In general, genetic information is read from DNA into RNA. This process is called transcription. The longer a gene is, the more time it takes to read from beginning to end. In addition, gene expression must be regulated at several steps. Neurons are therefore thought to require special mechanisms to read long genes accurately and stably, but the details of these mechanisms have remained unclear.

articles.title: The hole in the ozone layer is healing, but extreme weather may be slowing progress down
articles.description: Climate change, driven by humans, is making extreme weather more commonplace

articles.title: Study explores new photonics advance: Topology imprinting in nonlinear metasurfaces
articles.description: Light is traditionally described by properties such as wavelength, amplitude, phase and polarization. Advances in optics have shown that light can also be shaped into complex spatial patterns known as structured light, enabling new ways to carry information and interact with matter for applications in imaging, optical communications and information processing.

articles.title: UH telescope supports Euclid space mission
articles.description: The Euclid space mission incorporated data from UH ’s Pan- STARRS contributed data to create a map of the universe in 3D. The post UH telescope supports Euclid space mission first appeared on University of Hawaiʻi System News .

articles.description: Chinese researchers envision a nuclear-powered tank with a 50MJ railgun and a theoretical range of 280 miles.

articles.title: Potential dark matter detection sparks hope in search for elusive substance — and more UCLA media
articles.description: CNN reported on an intriguing signal detected by the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment that could offer a clue in the decades-long search for dark matter. UCLA physicist Alvine Kamaha, who helped build the detector, cautioned that one event is not enough to claim a discovery but said a confirmed detection would open “an entirely new area of particle physics.” Read more about UCLA in today’s Washington Post, The Conversation and others.
